Source pack (real public studies, read in full by the client team; cite only these ten and give findings as direction only, no invented numbers): Afridi (2010), Journal of Development Economics 92(2): in Madhya Pradesh school meals raised children's daily nutrient intake. Afridi (2011), Journal of Development Studies 47(11): school meals raised school participation in rural Madhya Pradesh. Jayaraman & Simroth (2015), Scandinavian Journal of Economics 117(4): primary enrolment rose after the scheme's rollout. Singh, Park & Dercon (2014), Economic Development and Cultural Change 62(2): in Andhra Pradesh the meal cushioned child nutrition against a drought shock. Chakraborty & Jayaraman (2019), Journal of Development Economics 139: meal access was linked to better reading and maths scores. Chakrabarti et al. (2021), Nature Communications 12: women who ate school meals as girls had children with better height-for-age. Khera (2006), Economic and Political Weekly 41(46): after the 2001 order, gains in attendance and equity but uneven meal quality and infrastructure. Dreze & Goyal (2003), Economic and Political Weekly 38(44): field evidence that cooked meals lifted attendance and weakened caste barriers. Policy anchors: Supreme Court interim order of 28 November 2001 in PUCL v. Union of India (cooked meals in government and aided primary schools); PM POSHAN guidelines (Ministry of Education, 2021).
samples.text:
Mid-day meals and school attendance in India since 2000: a thematic review of the evidence

1. Question, scope and method

This review asks what the available evidence shows about the effect of India's mid-day meal programme on school attendance, and on the outcomes through which attendance is expected to matter, so that a new pilot in Bihar knows what it must measure. The question is current because the programme now operates as PM POSHAN, whose 2021 guidelines keep cooked meals for children in government and government-aided schools in Classes I to VIII (Ministry of Education, 2021). Education officials and funders deciding where to add resources need to know which results are settled and which are not.

The national programme dates from 1995, but for years many states supplied dry rations instead of cooked meals. That changed with the Supreme Court's interim order of 28 November 2001 in PUCL v. Union of India, which required cooked meals in government and aided primary schools (Khera, 2006; PUCL v. Union of India, 2001). The review therefore covers evidence produced since 2000 and treats the 2001 order as the point from which the programme can be studied as a universal entitlement.

The method is deliberately narrow. This is a focused review, not a systematic one. It rests on ten sources that the research team read in full: eight studies published between 2003 and 2021, and two policy anchors, the 2001 order and the 2021 guidelines. A source was included if it concerned India's mid-day meal programme and reported on attendance, enrolment, nutrition, learning, equity or delivery. Findings are given as direction only, and effect sizes are left to the original papers. Because the review is not exhaustive, the absence of a study here should not be read as the absence of evidence. None of the ten sources, as described in the pack, is a Bihar evaluation.

2. Attendance, participation and learning

The evidence that cooked school meals raise children's presence in school points in one direction across the studies reviewed. Afridi (2011) found that school meals raised school participation in rural Madhya Pradesh. Jayaraman and Simroth (2015) found that primary enrolment rose after the scheme's rollout. Drèze and Goyal (2003) reported field evidence that cooked meals lifted attendance, and Khera (2006) recorded gains in attendance after the 2001 order.

The four findings are not interchangeable, and the differences matter for design. Enrolment counts children on the register, participation is a looser term whose definition the pack does not give, and attendance counts children in the classroom on a given day. A meal can bring a child onto the roll without changing how often the child sits in class, so a rise in enrolment does not by itself establish a rise in daily presence. Setting also differs. Afridi's result comes from rural Madhya Pradesh, and Jayaraman and Simroth's from the rollout of the scheme. The study by Drèze and Goyal was published within two years of the 2001 order, while Khera looks at the period after it. A programme in its early years and a programme after two decades may not behave alike.

The link from attendance to learning is thinner. Chakraborty and Jayaraman (2019) reported that meal access was linked to better reading and maths scores. One source cannot carry the claim that meals raise learning for children in Bihar, and the route from a fuller classroom to better scores is not explained in the finding as summarised. Taken together, the section supports a settled direction, more children in school more often where cooked meals are served, but not the size of the effect, its mechanism or its persistence. A pilot that reports enrolment alone would repeat the weakest link in this literature.

3. Nutrition

Three sources address nutrition, each at a different distance from the meal. Afridi (2010) found that in Madhya Pradesh school meals raised children's daily nutrient intake. Singh, Park and Dercon (2014) found that in Andhra Pradesh the meal cushioned child nutrition against a drought shock. Chakrabarti et al. (2021) found that women who ate school meals as girls had children with better height-for-age.

Read together, the three describe benefits at three horizons: what a child eats on a school day, how well a child's nutrition holds up when the household is under stress, and what is passed to the next generation. The agreement in direction is notable because the sources measure different things. Intake is a flow; height-for-age records accumulated growth. A rise in intake therefore does not prove a change in nutritional status, and the findings on status in this pack come from the protection offered during a shock and from the intergenerational result, not from the intake study. None of the three, as summarised in the pack, says whether the meal added to the food a child eats at home or displaced part of it. The full texts should be checked on this point before the pilot's measures are fixed.

The intergenerational finding carries a practical lesson. Because it operates through mothers, it suggests that benefits accumulate over a generation, which no pilot cycle can observe. A pilot can, however, record which children received meals and for how long, so that later follow-up becomes possible. The drought finding also leaves a question open: whether the meal protects against shocks other than drought, such as floods, is not answered by the evidence reviewed.

4. Social equity

The evidence on equity is the thinnest of the four themes. Drèze and Goyal (2003) reported that cooked meals weakened caste barriers, a finding that presupposes children eating together, which cooked meals served at school make possible and dry rations do not. Khera (2006) reported gains in equity after the 2001 order, alongside the uneven delivery discussed below. Chakrabarti et al. (2021) bear on equity indirectly, since their result concerns girls who later became mothers.

The sources use equity in different senses. Drèze and Goyal address caste, Khera reports gains in equity without the summary available here naming the group, and Chakrabarti et al. concern gender and the transmission of benefit across generations. The findings as summarised do not say whether attendance gains differ by caste, sex or household poverty, so they cannot show whether the children who gain most are those who were furthest from school. The direction of the evidence is favourable; its precision is low. For a state pilot, the implication is that equity cannot be assumed from the aggregate result. Attendance, meal uptake and who cooks and serves the meal would need to be recorded separately for children by social group and sex.

5. Implementation quality

Every result above describes the programme as it was delivered in its setting. Khera (2006) is the source that qualifies them, finding gains in attendance and equity but uneven meal quality and infrastructure after the 2001 order. The 2001 order established the entitlement, and the PM POSHAN guidelines set out how the programme is organised today (PUCL v. Union of India, 2001; Ministry of Education, 2021). Neither shows how well the entitlement is honoured in practice.

This leaves a gap between the programme on paper and the programme at the school gate. If quality and infrastructure are uneven, the effects reported by Afridi, by Jayaraman and Simroth, and by Chakraborty and Jayaraman are averages over schools that delivered differently. They may overstate what a poorly run school can expect or understate what a well-run one can achieve. None of the findings as summarised relates outcomes to the number of days meals are served, the quality of the meal, or the state of kitchens, water and storage. Delivery should therefore be treated in a Bihar pilot as an exposure to be measured, not as a background condition.

6. Limits of the evidence

Three features of how the question has been studied restrict what can be concluded. First, the sources answer different questions. One measures nutrient intake, another enrolment, another test scores, another the height of the next generation. No outcome is common to all of them, so the review can compare their direction but not their magnitude, and any claim that "the evidence shows an effect of a given size" would go beyond what is held here.

Second, the settings are narrow and uneven. The two sources set in a named state study Madhya Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh, and a third reports on schools soon after the 2001 order. Nothing in the pack describes Bihar's schools, its kitchens or its children, and findings from other states should be treated as hypotheses for Bihar, not as a forecast.

Third, the time horizons differ widely, from the years just after rollout to a generation later. A short pilot can speak to the first horizon only. Readers should therefore expect a pilot to confirm or qualify the near-term findings on attendance and delivery, and should not expect it to settle the long-run claims on nutrition.

7. Gaps for a Bihar pilot to test

The evidence supports a clear direction on attendance, nutrition and equity and leaves five questions that a pilot can answer.

First, daily attendance, as distinct from enrolment or participation, should be measured from registers and verified by unannounced visits, since two of the four attendance findings concern enrolment or participation.

Second, delivery should be recorded school by school: days on which a meal was served against days entitled, the meal actually served, and the condition of kitchen, water and storage. Outcomes can then be compared across levels of delivery, which the findings as summarised do not do.

Third, learning should be measured on a standard reading and maths tool, with a comparison group, because only one reviewed source speaks to scores.

Fourth, outcomes should be disaggregated by caste, sex and household poverty, so that the pilot reports who gains, not only how many.

Fifth, the pilot should record individual meal exposure in a way that permits later follow-up of nutrition, and should test whether meals protect against shocks beyond drought.

8. Conclusion

The question was what the evidence shows about mid-day meals and school attendance in India since 2000, and what a Bihar pilot must therefore measure. The evidence is consistent in direction: cooked school meals are associated with higher enrolment, participation and attendance, with better nutrition at several horizons, and with weaker caste barriers. It is much less consistent in precision. The size of the attendance effect, the route from attendance to learning, the benefit by social group and the dependence of all of these on delivery quality remain unsettled in the sources reviewed.

For a Bihar pilot, the gaps define the work. It should measure daily attendance, delivery, learning and the distribution of gains, none of which these sources settle, and it should leave a record that permits long-run follow-up. A pilot built this way would add to what is known; one that reports only enrolment would confirm what is already agreed.

References (titles, page ranges and DOIs to be checked against the journal records before release)

Afridi, F. (2011). The impact of school meals on school participation: Evidence from rural India. Journal of Development Studies, 47(11), 1636-1656.

Chakrabarti, S., Scott, S. P., Alderman, H., Menon, P., & Gilligan, D. O. (2021). Intergenerational nutrition benefits of India's national school feeding program. Nature Communications, 12, Article 4248.

Chakraborty, T., & Jayaraman, R. (2019). School feeding and learning achievement: Evidence from India's midday meal program. Journal of Development Economics, 139, 249-265.

Drèze, J., & Goyal, A. (2003). Future of mid-day meals. Economic and Political Weekly, 38(44), 4673-4683.

Jayaraman, R., & Simroth, D. (2015). The impact of school lunches on primary school enrollment: Evidence from India's midday meal scheme. Scandinavian Journal of Economics, 117(4), 1176-1203.

Khera, R. (2006). Mid-day meals in primary schools: Achievements and challenges. Economic and Political Weekly, 41(46), 4742-4750.

Ministry of Education. (2021). PM POSHAN guidelines. Government of India.

People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) v. Union of India (2001). Supreme Court of India, interim order of 28 November 2001.

SYNOPSIS (ICH E3, Section 2)
Clinical Study Report, Protocol HGP-AHT-301
Report date: 30 September 2026. Database lock: 14 September 2026.

Name of sponsor/company: [Sponsor name], Hyderabad, India
Name of finished product: Telmisartan 40 mg + amlodipine 5 mg fixed-dose combination (FDC)
Name of active ingredients: Telmisartan, amlodipine

Title of study: A 12-week, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled phase III study of telmisartan 40 mg + amlodipine 5 mg FDC versus telmisartan 40 mg, once daily, in adults with stage 2 essential hypertension.

Investigators: Principal investigators at 14 sites in India [names to be entered from the sponsor's investigator list].
Study centres: 14 sites in India.
Publication (reference): None.
Studied period: 12 January 2026 (first patient in) to 24 August 2026 (last patient last visit).
Phase of development: III

OBJECTIVES
Primary: to compare the change in seated systolic blood pressure (SBP) from baseline to week 12 between the FDC and telmisartan 40 mg alone.
Safety: to compare the safety and tolerability of the two treatments over 12 weeks.

METHODOLOGY
Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, active-controlled study. Patients were randomised to the FDC or to telmisartan 40 mg and treated for 12 weeks.

NUMBER OF PATIENTS
Planned: [number per protocol].
Randomised: 216 (FDC) and 214 (telmisartan 40 mg), 430 in total (Table 14.1.1).
Completed: 208 (FDC) and 205 (telmisartan 40 mg).
Analysed: the full analysis set and the safety set were each all randomised patients, 216 and 214.

DIAGNOSIS AND MAIN CRITERIA FOR INCLUSION
Adults with stage 2 essential hypertension [blood pressure thresholds and other criteria as defined in the protocol].

TEST PRODUCT, DOSE AND MODE OF ADMINISTRATION, BATCH NUMBER
Telmisartan 40 mg + amlodipine 5 mg FDC, oral, once daily. Batch number: [to be entered from the sponsor's batch records].

DURATION OF TREATMENT
12 weeks.

REFERENCE THERAPY, DOSE AND MODE OF ADMINISTRATION, BATCH NUMBER
Telmisartan 40 mg, oral, once daily. Batch number: [to be entered from the sponsor's batch records].

CRITERIA FOR EVALUATION
Efficacy: the primary endpoint was the change in seated SBP from baseline to week 12, measured as office blood pressure.
Safety: treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), serious adverse events (SAEs) and discontinuations due to adverse events.

STATISTICAL METHODS
The primary endpoint was analysed by analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) in the full analysis set. Least-squares (LS) means, the between-treatment difference and 95% confidence intervals (CI) are reported. Safety data are summarised as numbers and percentages of patients in the safety set, with the number randomised to each group (216 and 214) as the denominator. No hypothesis test is applied to the safety data. A negative change in SBP means a fall in blood pressure. Percentages are rounded to one decimal place.

SUMMARY OF RESULTS

Patient disposition. Of 430 patients randomised (216 FDC, 214 telmisartan), 413 completed the study (208 and 205). Eight FDC patients and 9 telmisartan patients discontinued. Reasons were adverse event (3 and 4), lost to follow-up (3 and 2) and consent withdrawn (2 and 3) (Table 14.1.1). Baseline seated SBP was 156.2 mmHg in the FDC group and 155.8 mmHg in the telmisartan group (Table 14.1.1).

Efficacy. At week 12 the LS-mean change in seated SBP was -18.4 mmHg (95% CI -20.2 to -16.6) with the FDC and -12.1 mmHg (95% CI -13.9 to -10.3) with telmisartan. The difference was -6.3 mmHg (95% CI -8.8 to -3.8), a greater reduction with the FDC (Table 14.2.1). The two groups started close together, 0.4 mmHg apart at baseline (156.2 and 155.8 mmHg), so the 6.3 mmHg difference at week 12 does not come from an imbalance at the start.

Safety. TEAEs occurred in 61 patients (28.2%) on the FDC and 52 (24.3%) on telmisartan. SAEs occurred in 2 patients (0.9%) and 3 patients (1.4%); none was drug-related. Adverse events led to discontinuation in 3 patients (1.4%) and 4 patients (1.9%). The most frequent TEAEs were:
- peripheral oedema: 14 (6.5%) FDC versus 3 (1.4%) telmisartan;
- headache: 11 (5.1%) versus 12 (5.6%);
- dizziness: 9 (4.2%) versus 8 (3.7%) (Table 14.3.1).
Of these three, peripheral oedema showed the largest difference between groups, 5.1 percentage points (6.5% versus 1.4%). The headache and dizziness differences were 0.5 percentage points each, in opposite directions. The discontinuations due to adverse events (3 and 4) match the adverse-event discontinuations in the disposition table (Table 14.1.1).

RESULTS AT A GLANCE (every value is taken from the CSR table named in the last column)

Parameter | FDC (n = 216) | Telmisartan (n = 214) | Source
Randomised | 216 | 214 | Table 14.1.1
Completed | 208 | 205 | Table 14.1.1
Discontinued, total | 8 | 9 | Table 14.1.1
Adverse event | 3 | 4 | Table 14.1.1
Lost to follow-up | 3 | 2 | Table 14.1.1
Consent withdrawn | 2 | 3 | Table 14.1.1
Baseline seated SBP, mmHg | 156.2 | 155.8 | Table 14.1.1
LS-mean change in seated SBP at week 12, mmHg (95% CI) | -18.4 (-20.2 to -16.6) | -12.1 (-13.9 to -10.3) | Table 14.2.1
Difference, FDC minus telmisartan, mmHg (95% CI) | -6.3 (-8.8 to -3.8) | | Table 14.2.1
TEAEs, n (%) | 61 (28.2) | 52 (24.3) | Table 14.3.1
SAEs, n (%) | 2 (0.9) | 3 (1.4) | Table 14.3.1
Adverse-event discontinuations, n (%) | 3 (1.4) | 4 (1.9) | Table 14.3.1
Peripheral oedema, n (%) | 14 (6.5) | 3 (1.4) | Table 14.3.1
Headache, n (%) | 11 (5.1) | 12 (5.6) | Table 14.3.1
Dizziness, n (%) | 9 (4.2) | 8 (3.7) | Table 14.3.1

CONCLUSIONS

Efficacy. After 12 weeks the FDC lowered seated SBP by 6.3 mmHg more than telmisartan 40 mg alone. The 95% CI for the difference (-8.8 to -3.8 mmHg) does not include zero.

Safety. TEAEs were reported by 28.2% of patients on the FDC and 24.3% on telmisartan. SAEs were few in both groups and none was drug-related. Peripheral oedema was reported more often with the FDC (6.5% versus 1.4%), while headache and dizziness occurred at similar rates in the two groups. Discontinuations due to adverse events were 3 and 4 patients.

Limitations. The study lasted 12 weeks, so it cannot show longer-term efficacy or safety. Blood pressure was measured in the office only, with no ambulatory or home readings. There was no placebo arm, and no arm for amlodipine 5 mg alone, so the effect against placebo and the separate contribution of each component were not assessed.

Date of the report: 30 September 2026.

# GST for D2C brands in India: what to register, file and claim

A D2C brand in India needs a GST registration in every state where it stores stock, and it can claim input tax credit (ITC) only on purchase invoices that show up in GSTR-2B. Beyond that, it needs proper invoices and regular GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B returns. Once turnover has crossed Rs 5 crore, invoices to business customers must also be e-invoiced. This page is for D2C founders doing Rs 1-50 crore in revenue. It walks through the five GST jobs below, helps you choose a filing scheme, answers the questions we hear most often, and links to our full article on each topic.

## On this page

- [GST registration: when and where](#registration)
- [E-invoicing: does your turnover trigger it?](#e-invoicing)
- [GST on marketplace sales](#marketplace)
- [Input tax credit: claim only what GSTR-2B shows](#itc)
- [GST notices: read, reconcile, reply](#notices)
- [Which GST scheme fits your brand](#scheme)
- [Six questions D2C founders ask](#faq)
- [Book a 15-minute GST health-check call](#next-step)

## The five GST jobs of a D2C brand

1. **Register** in the state you sell from and in each state where stock is kept.
2. **Invoice** every sale properly; e-invoice business sales once turnover crosses Rs 5 crore.
3. **Report** sales and tax in GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B, on the due dates the GST portal shows.
4. **Claim** input tax credit on purchases that appear in GSTR-2B, before the 30 November cut-off.
5. **Respond** to any notice by the date printed on it, which is often 30 days.

## GST registration: when and where {#registration}

A seller of goods must register once yearly turnover crosses Rs 40 lakh in most states. At Rs 1 crore or more you are well past that line, so the harder question is where. GST registration is state-wise. Each state registration is a separate GSTIN with its own returns, though every GSTIN carries your PAN inside it. Turnover for the Rs 40 lakh test, and for every limit further down this page, is added up across all your GSTINs under one PAN. A brand with GSTINs in four states and Rs 1.5 crore of sales in each is a Rs 6 crore brand.

If a marketplace keeps your stock in a warehouse in another state, that warehouse is a place of business and needs a registration in that state. The state also decides your tax type on every consumer sale. Goods delivered inside the state of your registration carry CGST and SGST. Goods delivered to another state carry IGST. Your own website and each marketplace need the right GSTIN on the right order. Full guide: [GST registration for D2C brands](/gst-registration-d2c).

## E-invoicing: does your turnover trigger it? {#e-invoicing}

E-invoicing applies once your aggregate turnover has crossed Rs 5 crore in any financial year since 2017-18. It does not switch off if turnover later dips. It covers invoices, credit notes and debit notes to registered businesses, and exports. Sales to individual consumers are outside it.

Each covered invoice must get an invoice reference number (IRN) and a QR code from the government's Invoice Registration Portal before it goes to the buyer. An invoice without an IRN is not treated as a valid invoice, which puts your business customer's input tax credit at risk. For a D2C brand this usually means wholesale, bulk and corporate-gifting invoices, not consumer orders. Full guide: [how e-invoicing works for D2C brands](/e-invoicing-d2c).

## GST on marketplace sales {#marketplace}

A marketplace is an e-commerce operator under GST. It collects tax at source (TCS) under section 52 on your net taxable sales and deposits it with the government, while you still report the sales in your own GSTR-1. With two marketplaces you have two sets of TCS figures, so compare what each one deducted against its own settlement report every month.

Two other items belong in the same monthly check. First, the marketplace's commission, fulfilment and advertising invoices carry GST of their own, and that GST is ITC you can claim once it shows in GSTR-2B. Second, returns matter: a credit note for a returned order must be declared by 30 November after the financial year of the sale, or the tax you paid on that sale cannot be adjusted. Full guide: [GST on marketplace sales](/gst-marketplace-sales).

## Input tax credit: claim only what GSTR-2B shows {#itc}

ITC lets you set off the GST you paid on purchases, such as packaging, ad services and freight, against the GST you collect on sales. You can claim a purchase invoice when three things are true. It appears in your GSTR-2B, the goods or services were received, and your supplier has paid the tax. Invoices of a financial year must be claimed by 30 November after it ends, or the date you file the annual return, whichever is earlier. For 2025-26 invoices that is 30 November 2026. Credit on goods given away as free samples is blocked under section 17(5)(h), so do not claim it.

The routine that protects you is simple. Before filing GSTR-3B each month, compare your purchase register with GSTR-2B. An invoice that is missing usually means the supplier has not filed GSTR-1 yet or quoted the wrong GSTIN. Chase it that month, not in November.

**A case from our files.** A Rs 6 crore skincare brand, selling on two marketplaces and its own site, found Rs 9.4 lakh of unclaimed ITC because 14 suppliers' invoices were missing from GSTR-2B. It recovered Rs 7.1 lakh before the 30 November cut-off, about three quarters of the total. Full guide: [claiming input tax credit as a D2C brand](/input-tax-credit-d2c).

## GST notices: read, reconcile, reply {#notices}

A common trigger for a notice is a mismatch between GSTR-1, what you reported as sales, and GSTR-3B, what you paid tax on. A scrutiny notice in Form ASMT-10 gives 30 days to reply, and the officer can extend that. Your first response should follow four steps:

1. Note the notice number, date, section and due date.
2. Download GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B for the period named.
3. Reconcile them month by month and find the cause of the gap.
4. Reply on the portal with the working attached, well before the due date.

**A case from our files.** A Rs 3 crore apparel brand received a notice over a Rs 2.2 lakh mismatch between GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B. It replied with a reconciliation on day 15 of the 30 allowed, and the matter closed with no demand. Full guide: [how to reply to a GST notice](/gst-notice-reply).

## Which GST scheme fits your brand {#scheme}

| | Regular, monthly | Regular with QRMP | Composition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Turnover limit | None | Up to Rs 5 crore in the previous financial year | Up to Rs 1.5 crore in the previous year (most states) |
| Returns | GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B every month | GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B every quarter, tax paid monthly | CMP-08 every quarter, GSTR-4 once a year |
| Tax paid | Normal rates, less ITC | Normal rates, less ITC | Flat 1% of turnover for goods traders and manufacturers |
| Input tax credit | Yes | Yes | No |
| Sales to other states | Allowed | Allowed | Not allowed |
| Best fit | Brands above Rs 5 crore, or anyone who wants monthly control | Brands up to Rs 5 crore that want fewer filings | Rarely a D2C fit |

Choose in this order. Start with turnover, because QRMP is open only up to Rs 5 crore and composition only up to Rs 1.5 crore. Then look at where you ship: composition shuts out any seller who delivers to customers in another state, which is most D2C brands. Last, decide between monthly and quarterly filing. QRMP means fewer returns, but you still pay tax every month, and a brand close to Rs 5 crore should plan now for e-invoicing and monthly returns.

## Six questions D2C founders ask {#faq}

**Do I need GST registration if I only sell on marketplaces?**
Yes, in practice. A brand with Rs 1 crore or more in sales is past the Rs 40 lakh goods threshold, and marketplaces ask for a GSTIN before they let you list most goods.

**Do I need a GSTIN in every state where a marketplace stores my stock?**
Yes. A warehouse holding your stock is a place of business in that state, so you need a registration there and file returns under that GSTIN too.

**Does e-invoicing apply to my consumer orders?**
No. It covers invoices to registered businesses and exports, plus related credit and debit notes. Your sales to individual customers are outside it.

**What is the last date to claim ITC on 2025-26 purchase invoices?**
30 November 2026, or the date you file your 2025-26 annual return if that comes first. Check GSTR-2B for missing invoices well before that.

**What if a supplier's invoice is missing from GSTR-2B?**
You cannot claim it until it appears. Ask the supplier to file their GSTR-1. The invoice then shows in your GSTR-2B for that period, and you can claim it, provided you are still within the 30 November deadline.

**How long do I have to reply to a GST notice?**
Read the due date printed on the notice first. A scrutiny notice in Form ASMT-10 gives 30 days, and the officer can extend it. Reply on the portal with a reconciliation and supporting documents.

## Not sure which of this applies to your brand? {#next-step}

Book a 15-minute GST health-check call with Mehta & Rathore Associates: [booking link to be added]. Or start with the article that matches your question, such as [GST registration for D2C brands](/gst-registration-d2c).

रैली भाषण (10 मिनट): कल का सारण, आज का सारण

वक्ता: विधायक रामनाथ सिंह, जन विकास मोर्चा
मतदान: मंगलवार, 17 नवंबर 2026 | चुनाव निशान: कलश
वक्ता के लिए: (विराम) का मतलब रुककर भीड़ को जवाब देने देना है। [नारा] वाले हिस्से भीड़ के साथ बोले जाएँगे। [वैकल्पिक कटौती] वाले हिस्से समय कम पड़ने पर छोड़े जा सकते हैं।

1. सलाम और अपनापन (डेढ़ मिनट)

रउआ सब के गोड़ लागीं। (हाथ जोड़कर)

मंच पर बैठे बड़े-बुजुर्गो, पार्टी के साथियो, माई-बहिन लोग, और मेरे नौजवान भाइयो-बहनो।

का हाल बा, सारण? (विराम)

सब ठीक बा नू? रउआ सब के देखके हमार मन हरियर हो गइल।

यह भिखारी ठाकुर की धरती है। उन्होंने हमारी ही बोली में, हमारे ही गाँव-घर की बात कही। आज मैं भी उसी बोली में आपके सामने हिसाब देने आया हूँ।

मेरा नाम आप जानते हैं। रामनाथ सिंह। आपने मुझे विधायक बनाया। आज मैं आपके सामने रिपोर्ट कार्ड लेकर खड़ा हूँ।

यहाँ पहली बार वोट देने वाले नौजवान बैठे हैं। यहाँ स्वयं सहायता समूह की दीदियाँ बैठी हैं। आज की बात सबसे पहले आपसे है।

2. एक ही बात: कल का सारण, आज का सारण (डेढ़ मिनट)

आज मैं एक ही बात लेकर आया हूँ। कल का सारण, आज का सारण।

कल का सारण आप जानते हैं। आपने उसे जिया है। आज का सारण भी आपके सामने है। आप रोज उस पर चलते हैं।

दोनों के बीच जो फर्क है, वह मेरे भाषण से नहीं दिखता। वह आपकी अपनी आँख से दिखता है।

आज के सारण को ध्यान से देखिए। फिर आगे के सारण की सोचिए। जहाँ कोई गाँव अलग-थलग न रहे। कोई बेटी कॉलेज के दरवाजे पर न रुके। कोई दीदी अकेली न पड़े। उस सारण की शुरुआत आज के सारण से ही होती है।

इसलिए आज मैं भाषण नहीं दूँगा। हिसाब दूँगा। किलोमीटर में। करोड़ रुपये में। विद्यार्थियों की गिनती में।

और हर हिसाब के बाद आपसे एक बात पूछूँगा। जवाब आपको देना है।

3. हिसाब: सड़क, कॉलेज, दीदियाँ (चार मिनट)

पहले सड़क।

कोठिया से रघुनाथपुर तक स्टेट हाईवे। 28 किलोमीटर। 142 करोड़ रुपये। साल 2022 में काम पूरा। (विराम)

फिर बेलौरी से गंगा घाट तक की सड़क। 19 किलोमीटर। 96 करोड़ रुपये। साल 2024 में काम पूरा।

दोनों जोड़ लीजिए। 47 किलोमीटर। 238 करोड़ रुपये।

यानी हर किलोमीटर पर करीब 5 करोड़ रुपये। यह पैसा सड़क में लगा है, और सड़क आपके पैरों के नीचे है।

गंगा घाट तक जाने वाले लोग, बीमार को शहर ले जाने वाले परिवार, मंडी तक अनाज पहुँचाने वाले किसान, वही बताएँगे कि अब रास्ता कैसा है। मुझे कुछ कहने की जरूरत नहीं।

[नारा 1] मैं पूछूँगा, आप जवाब देंगे। (विराम)
मैं पूछूँगा: सड़क? आप कहेंगे: बनल!
मैं पूछूँगा: गाँव? आप कहेंगे: जुड़ल!
एक बार फिर। सड़क? (बनल!) गाँव? (जुड़ल!)

अब पढ़ाई की बात।

बेलौरी में सरकारी डिग्री कॉलेज। साल 2021 में खुला। आज उसमें 1,850 विद्यार्थी पढ़ रहे हैं।

इनमें 851 बेटियाँ हैं। यानी 46 फीसदी। यानी हर सौ विद्यार्थियों में 46 बेटियाँ।

[वैकल्पिक कटौती: अगले तीन वाक्य, लगभग आधा मिनट]
यहाँ जो माताएँ बैठी हैं, उनमें से कई की बेटी आज उस कॉलेज में पढ़ रही होगी। उसकी पढ़ाई आपकी जीत है। मेरी नहीं।
[कटौती यहाँ खत्म]

[नारा 2] मैं पूछूँगा: कॉलेज? आप कहेंगे: खुलल!
मैं पूछूँगा: बेटी? आप कहेंगे: पढ़त बा!
एक बार फिर। कॉलेज? (खुलल!) बेटी? (पढ़त बा!)

अब दीदियों की बात।

हमारे यहाँ 1,240 स्वयं सहायता समूह हैं। इनमें 14,880 महिलाएँ सदस्य हैं। यानी हर समूह में औसतन 12 बहनें।

इन समूहों को बैंक से 38 करोड़ रुपये का कर्ज मिला है। यानी हर समूह के पास औसतन करीब 3 लाख रुपये, और हर सदस्य के हिस्से में करीब 25,500 रुपये।

[वैकल्पिक कटौती: अगले दो वाक्य, लगभग 20 सेकंड]
यह आँकड़ा कागज का नहीं है। अपने समूह की दीदी से पूछ लीजिए।
[कटौती यहाँ खत्म]

सड़क, कॉलेज और दीदियों का कर्ज। तीनों का हिसाब मैंने आपके सामने रख दिया।

मैं यह नहीं कहता कि सब हो गया। काम अभी बाकी है। हर गाँव, हर टोले तक पक्की सड़क शायद अभी नहीं पहुँची। हर बेटी अभी कॉलेज तक नहीं पहुँची। हर बहन अभी किसी समूह से नहीं जुड़ी। यह सच है, और मैं इसे मानता हूँ।

लेकिन आज का सवाल बदल गया है। अब सवाल यह है कि अगली सड़क किस गाँव की होगी। अगली बेटी किस कॉलेज में जाएगी। अगली दीदी किस समूह से जुड़ेगी। सवाल का बदल जाना ही आज का सारण है।

4. हिसाब माँगने की बात (डेढ़ मिनट)

[वैकल्पिक कटौती: पूरा यह हिस्सा, लगभग डेढ़ मिनट]

मैंने अपना हिसाब रख दिया। अब मैं बस इतना चाहता हूँ कि बाकी लोग भी अपना हिसाब रखें।

अपने समय का। अपने नाम से। किलोमीटर में, करोड़ में, विद्यार्थियों की गिनती में।

न किसी के घर-परिवार की बात, न किसी की जात-बिरादरी की। हमारी बात काम की है।

जो हिसाब दिखाए, आप उसकी सुनिए। जो न दिखाए, उससे सवाल कीजिए। यह आपका हक है।

[कटौती यहाँ खत्म]

5. आगे की बात: तीन काम, एक वादा (ढाई मिनट)

अब आगे की बात। तीन काम। और एक वादा।

पहला काम, सड़क। 47 किलोमीटर पर मैं रुकूँगा नहीं। जिस गाँव तक अभी पक्की सड़क नहीं पहुँची, उसकी सूची आपके साथ बैठकर बनेगी। फिर हर साल उस सूची से गाँव जुड़ते जाएँगे।

दूसरा काम, कॉलेज। आज 46 फीसदी बेटियाँ हैं। यह गिनती और ऊपर जाए, यही मेरा लक्ष्य है। रास्ते की रुकावट हो, फीस की हो या डर की हो, जिस वजह से बेटी की पढ़ाई रुके, वह वजह आपके साथ मिलकर हटाऊँगा।

तीसरा काम, दीदियाँ। आज 1,240 समूह हैं। जो बहनें अभी किसी समूह से बाहर हैं, वे भी जुड़ें। अगली बार जब आपके सामने आऊँगा, यह गिनती 1,240 से बड़ी होगी।

और वादा एक। हर साल आपके बीच आकर इसी तरह हिसाब दूँगा। किलोमीटर में। करोड़ में। गिनती में।

# Airvana Home 300 review: 30 days in a Delhi November

**Verdict:** Buy the Airvana Home 300 for a closed bedroom of about 130 sq ft. With the door shut, our bedroom averaged 38 µg/m³ of PM2.5 in the morning and 55 at night, against 268 and 341 outdoors. Skip it if you need an app that stays connected, or if your room is bigger than the 330 sq ft the maker claims. For larger rooms, look at the Purewind Max 500. We paid Rs 10,499 on 1 November 2025. Price checked on 1 December 2025: Rs 10,299 on Amazon.in.

**Disclosure:** We bought this unit ourselves for Rs 10,499 on Saturday 1 November 2025, so the maker had no say in this review. The two buying links near the end are affiliate links to Amazon.in and the maker's store, and the blog may earn a commission if you buy through them.

## How we tested

We ran the Airvana Home 300 from 1 to 30 November 2025 in a 132 sq ft bedroom of a 2BHK flat in Dwarka, Delhi. The door stayed shut and the purifier ran in auto mode, about 16 hours a day. We measured PM2.5 with a handheld monitor, outdoors and in the bedroom, in the morning and at night, and noted the averages for each. We measured noise at 1 m on every setting.

The maker rates the unit for up to 330 sq ft, so our bedroom is 40% of its rated area. We did not test that upper limit. We also have no reading from the same bedroom with the purifier switched off, so the numbers below describe the air in the room, not the purifier's effect on its own.

## Air quality: a shut bedroom against a Delhi November

What we expected: a 132 sq ft room is 40% of the rated area, so we expected this to be an easy job for the unit. What we measured: outdoors, the monitor averaged 268 µg/m³ of PM2.5 in the morning and 341 at night. In the bedroom, with the purifier in auto mode, the averages were 38 in the morning and 55 at night. That is about 86% lower than outdoors in the morning and about 84% lower at night. The bedroom reading rose at night along with the outdoor one.

For context, India's 24-hour standard for PM2.5 is 60 µg/m³ and the World Health Organization's 2021 guideline is 15. Both bedroom readings sit under the Indian standard and above the WHO figure. Ours are morning and night averages, not 24-hour means. They also come from a handheld monitor, which is less exact than a reference instrument. Treat the comparison as a guide and not a certificate.

What it means: in a small closed bedroom, the room stayed far below the outdoor level through a month that is heavy on pollution in Delhi. What it does not tell you is how the unit copes in a room at the top of its rating. Our room used 40% of the claimed area.

## Noise: four settings measured at 1 m

What we expected: a quiet sleep setting and a clear step up with each speed. Sleep mode measured 28 dB at 1 m. Low measured 36, medium 47 and high 58. From low upwards, each step adds 11 dB, and a rise of about 10 dB is commonly heard as roughly twice as loud. So medium is not a small step up from low, and high is not a setting you will want running while you talk or sleep in the same room.

What it means: use sleep mode in the bedroom, and treat high as a setting for when you are out of the room. In auto mode the unit chooses the fan speed, so how loud it gets depends on how dirty the air is that day.

## Filter and running cost

What we expected: an indicator that roughly tracks the 6-month rating. The replacement filter costs Rs 2,400 and the maker rates it for 6 months. After our 30 days, the filter indicator showed 22% used. At that pace the filter would be used up in about 136 days, or 4.5 months, short of the 6-month rating.

On paper the filter costs Rs 400 a month (Rs 2,400 over 6 months). At our November pace it comes to about Rs 530 a month (Rs 2,400 over 4.5 months). Two cautions apply. The indicator is the maker's estimate, and we have one month of data. Delhi in November is a heavy-pollution month, so a full year may come closer to the rating. Treat Rs 400 as the floor and Rs 530 as the figure for a bad winter.

We did not measure electricity use, so this running cost covers the filter only.

## App and firmware

This is where the Airvana Home 300 let us down. We expected an app that holds its connection. Instead it lost its Wi-Fi connection after every router restart, and we re-paired the purifier three times in the month. Then the firmware update on day 19, which was 19 November, reset our schedules.

What it means: if you want schedules and remote control, expect to look after the app. If you plan to leave the purifier in auto mode and ignore the app, these faults will cost you less. Either way, note them before you buy.

## What the first year costs

Price first. The maker's store charged Rs 10,999 on 1 December 2025, Rs 700 more than the Rs 10,299 on Amazon.in. We paid Rs 10,499 on 1 November.

Then the filter. Assume the filter in the box is the first one. At the maker's 6-month rating you would buy one replacement in year one, for Rs 2,400. At our November pace of about 136 days per filter you would buy two, for Rs 4,800. Add the Amazon.in price and the first year costs between Rs 12,699 and Rs 15,099, before electricity, which we did not measure. Over a long winter in Delhi, plan for the higher figure.

## What we could not test

A month in one flat leaves gaps, and you should know them before you rely on our numbers. We tested one unit in one bedroom. We have no purifier-off reading for that room, so we cannot say how much of the drop from outdoors comes from the purifier and how much from a shut door. We did not push the unit toward its 330 sq ft rating. We did not measure electricity use. We saw one month of filter wear, and that month was November. We will add to the update log if the filter lasts longer in cleaner months or if a later firmware update fixes the app.

## Pros and cons

**Pros**
- Bedroom averages of 38 µg/m³ in the morning and 55 at night, door shut, against 268 and 341 outdoors.
- 28 dB at 1 m in sleep mode.
- A filter indicator that gave us a figure to work with: 22% used after 30 days.
- Rs 10,299 on Amazon.in on 1 December 2025, Rs 200 below what we paid.

**Cons**
- The app dropped Wi-Fi after every router restart: 3 re-pairs in 30 days.
- Schedules reset after the day-19 firmware update.
- The filter used 22% in 30 days, a 4.5-month pace against a 6-month rating, about Rs 530 a month in November air.
- Loud on high: 58 dB at 1 m.
- We did not test it in a room near its 330 sq ft rating.

## Alternatives

The one alternative we can name is the Purewind Max 500, at Rs 18,500 and rated for 650 sq ft. We have not tested it, and we have not tested any other purifier for this review, so we name only one. Buy it instead of the Airvana if your room is bigger than 330 sq ft.

The comparison rests on the makers' ratings, not on our tests. By those ratings the Purewind costs about Rs 8,000 more than we paid for the Airvana, but covers almost twice the area. That works out to roughly Rs 28 per square foot of rated area, against roughly Rs 32 for the Airvana. If you have a big room and are tempted to stretch the Airvana, the ratings favour the Purewind.

## Who should buy, who should skip

Buy it if you want to clean the air in one closed bedroom of up to about 130 sq ft. It suits you if you will mostly use sleep and auto modes and can live with an unreliable app.

Skip it if you need a purifier for a living room or a hall near 330 sq ft or larger. Skip it if you rely on app schedules. Skip it too if you do not want a filter that may need replacing in about 4.5 months in a bad winter.

## Final verdict and where to buy

We would buy it again for a small bedroom and would not buy it for a big room. The air results were good, the noise was manageable and the filter cost is clear, but the app is poor. Prices below were checked on Monday 1 December 2025.

- Amazon.in: Rs 10,299 [affiliate link]
- The maker's store: Rs 10,999 [affiliate link]

## Update log

1 December 2025: prices rechecked. Rs 10,299 on Amazon.in and Rs 10,999 on the maker's store.

In a cold room near Gaya, tomatoes wait ten days and fetch more than double

A solar-powered cooperative of vegetable growers opens its third storage unit on 16 November. Its members say storage has changed what they earn. A block officer and a mandi agent each name a problem it leaves open.

Ramchandra Manjhi's tomatoes were worth Rs 6 a kilo on the day he picked them. Ten days later, after a stay in a cold room near Gaya, the same tomatoes were worth Rs 14.

"Pehle tomato sadne se pehle bechna padta tha," Manjhi says. "Ab bhaav ka intezaar kar sakte hain." (Translated from Hindi: Before, we had to sell the tomatoes before they rotted. Now we can wait for the price.)

The cold room belongs to a cooperative founded by Anita Kumari, 41. On Monday 16 November 2026 it opens its third unit, ahead of the winter vegetable harvest.

That gap between Rs 6 and Rs 14 is the story. Tomatoes and cauliflower are perishable, and for a small grower harvest day usually means selling at whatever price the mandi offers, because the crop will not wait. A cold room lets the farmer wait. But a cold room does not solve everything. Outside winter the cooperative's units run at 60% of capacity, and the people who know the market best name more than one thing it has not fixed.

**From the mandi to a cooperative**

Anita Kumari is from a village near Gaya. She completed a B.Sc. in Gaya in 2006 and married in 2007. From 2012 to 2018 she sold vegetables at the Gaya mandi, the wholesale market where growers sell through commission agents. She says she watched about a third of her stock rot each summer.

In 2019, a year after she left the mandi, she founded the cooperative with 24 farmers. Seven years later it has 86 members. That is 62 more in seven years, about nine a year.

The storage came in three steps. The first unit, of 10 tonnes, opened in 2021. A 15-tonne unit followed in 2023. The third, of 25 tonnes, is as large as the first two together and brings the total to 50 tonnes. The gaps between units are two years, then three. Members pay Rs 1.5 a kilo a month to store their produce. For example, 100 kilos stored for the full month cost Rs 150.

**What a cold room does to a price**

The numbers farmers give are specific. Manjhi's tomatoes fetched Rs 6 a kilo on harvest day and Rs 14 after 10 days in store. Sunita Devi, who grows cauliflower, got Rs 8 at harvest and Rs 17 after 12 days. Both prices more than doubled. Spread over the days in store, the rise is about 80 paise a kilo a day for the tomatoes and about 75 paise for the cauliflower. A day in store costs 5 paise a kilo at Rs 1.5 a month. The rise will not have been a straight line, and the farmers quoted only the two ends.

Storage is not free, so the gain is smaller than the headline gap. A month's fee is Rs 1.5 a kilo. Even if a member is charged the full month, that leaves Manjhi at least Rs 6.5 a kilo better off than he would have been on harvest day, and Sunita Devi at least Rs 7.5. Put in rupees for a small lot: on Manjhi's figures, 100 kilos of tomatoes gain Rs 800 over ten days, against a fee of at most Rs 150, so the member keeps at least Rs 650. These are two members' own figures, not an average across 86 members, and prices on any given day depend on the mandi. The prices are the farmers' own. The unit sizes, fee and membership come from the cooperative, and the district numbers come from the block officer.

The fee also pays for the cooperative itself. At 50 tonnes, with every kilo paying a full month, fees would come to Rs 75,000 a month. At the 60% the units run outside winter, that falls to Rs 45,000. This is the reporter's arithmetic, not a figure from the cooperative.

Space is the other number to watch. Before the third unit, 25 tonnes shared among 86 members came to about 290 kilos each. The new unit lifts that to about 580 if everyone stored at once. A member with more than that to sell would still have to sell part of the crop on harvest day.

**The doubts**

Two people who know the district and the market have doubts, and the cooperative's own figures back some of them.

Dinesh Prasad, the block agriculture officer, puts the cooperative in a district-wide picture. Gaya district has 31 cold stores, he says, and only 4 of them are for vegetables. That is about one in eight.

"Small units lift prices for members, but without a buyer link they run half-empty," Dinesh Prasad says.

A buyer link, as the phrase is usually understood, is an arrangement under which someone has agreed to take the stored produce. Without one, a farmer who waits can end up waiting with nobody to sell to.

His "half-empty" is a figure of speech. The cooperative's own figure is 60% of capacity outside winter, which means 40% empty. At that rate, 50 tonnes would mean 30 tonnes in use and 20 empty.

Power is the second limit. The units run on solar power, and two cloudy days last January needed diesel backup that cost Rs 4,800. That is Rs 2,400 a day on a day without sun, paid out of fees that depend on how full the rooms are.

Lallan Prasad has a different worry. He has been a commission agent at the Gaya mandi for 22 years, and agents earn a commission on what passes through the market.

"Maal ruk jayega to aamad ghategi," he says. "Kisan ko aaj paisa chahiye; udhaar ka byaj kaun dega?" (Translated: If the produce is held back, arrivals will fall. The farmer needs money today; who will pay the interest on the loan?)

His point rests on how a mandi sets prices. On a day when many farmers arrive with the same crop, the price falls. On a day when fewer arrive, it rises. A cooperative that holds produce back takes arrivals out of that day's market. That is how cold storage can lift prices for its members, and it is why an agent hears it as a threat to his volumes. Whether it lifts prices for anyone outside the cooperative is not something these figures show.

His question points at a real trade-off. A farmer who waits ten days for Rs 14 still has household costs, and any credit he has taken keeps running. The figures above do not show how members bridge that wait. That is the part of the cold-room model they cannot yet answer.

The third unit does not settle it. It adds 25 tonnes of space, and whether the buyer link Dinesh Prasad describes arrives to fill it is still open. The next test comes outside winter, when the units have so far run at 60%.

Sunita Devi, who sold her cauliflower at Rs 17 after 12 days in store, has a simpler way of putting it.

"Ab mandi mein bhaav hum batate hain, pehle sunte the," she says. (Translated: Now at the mandi we name the price. Before, we only listened.)
